paper_title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

Introduction Figure 1 (a) An example from PMC-VQA [55], where Qwen3.5-4B writes 1,024 tokens without selecting an option and MedJev-4B scores the candidates in one forward pass. (b) Per-request latency against generated tokens, thinking off. (c) Average accuracy and latency on four benchmarks, where MedJev-4B beats all 20 general and medical VLMs at the 4B9B scale on both. Vision-language models (VLMs) have become general interface for understanding medical images. Both general-purpose VLMs [3, 4, 24, 43, 58] and medical VLMs trained on biomedical image-text MedJev data [5, 20, 34, 48] can read dermoscopy images, radiographs, and biomedical figures and answer clinical questions about them in natural language. Going one step further, recent medical VLMs are trained to write out their reasoning traces before giving the final answer [17, 29]. For all of these models, obtaining the result of medical image task relies on autoregressive generation and decoding. This autoregressive process is an expensive and indirect way to obtain these results. Each generated token requires another forward pass through the language model, so the inference cost grows with the length of the response (Fig. 1 (b)), and reasoning traces make the response much longer. Even with thinking disabled, the original Qwen3.5-4B [31] answers typical question of the multi-image benchmark MedThinkVQA [52] in 0.35 in our measurements, yet its 95th-percentile latency exceeds 20 and its mean latency reaches 1.84 s. Beyond this cost, the decision has to be parsed from free-form text with rules or an extra model, and response that matches none of the candidates is counted as an error (Fig. 1 (a)). Moreover, the reasoning traces contribute little, as more than 70% of model errors on MedThinkVQA come from reading the images and integrating evidence across views, and and longer traces help little once this grounding is weak [52]. The above two problems both stem from producing the decision as generated text. Dual-process theories of cognition describe two modes of thinking, fast and intuitive system one and slow and deliberate system two [9, 15]. Inspired by this theory, Jev models [2] have quickly become popular, mainly because they give up free-form generation and return typed and probabilistic decisions directly, which removes both the decoding cost and the output parsing. Many medical image tasks ask for one choice among fixed set of diagnoses or answers, which matches this form of decision making. We therefore aim to understand medical images in system one manner and propose MedJev-4B, fast and effective vision-language decision model built on Qwen3.5-4B. Given one or more medical images, question, and set of candidate answers, MedJev appends marker token to each candidate and decision token to the end of the input, scores all candidates jointly in single forward pass, and takes the highest-scoring candidate as its prediction. Since no reasoning or answer tokens are generated, the decision cost no longer grows with the response length, and prediction is always valid. The core idea of MedJev is to make the decision with less language-side computation while keeping all visual evidence and the matching structure learned in pretraining. It realizes this idea with two complementary designs, language-side depth reduction that shortens the path from the visual evidence to the decision for speed, and residual decision head that refines pretrained querykey matching for accuracy on the heterogeneous medical decisions. Language-Side Depth Reduction. Starting from pretrained VLM, MedJev keeps the vision encoder, the vision-language connector, and every visual token that they produce. Since studies of large language models find that many of the deepest layers can be removed with limited loss in performance [10, 27], it removes the language-side computation that the decision does not use, namely the upper layers before the last one, the value, gate, output, and feed-forward paths of the last layer, and the vocabulary projection. In MedJev-4B, these components account for 20% of the parameters. Visual token pruning methods [6, 47, 56] accelerate VLMs by discarding encoded visual tokens, which may remove small lesions and fine structures. MedJev therefore keeps the visual evidence intact and shortens only the language-side path to the decision. Residual Decision Head. To score the candidates, MedJev reuses the query and key projections of the last layer, which already learned in pretraining how strongly one token attends to another. It maps the decision token to query and each candidate marker to key, and takes their scaled dot product as the matching score of the candidate. Because pretrained matching alone may not be expressive enough for heterogeneous medical images and questions, lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) shared across candidates adds residual score computed from the decision state, the candidate state, and their elementwise product. Its output layer is initialized to zero, so training starts from pretrained 2 MedJev matching and learns task-specific nonlinear discrimination with few new parameters. Extensive experiments on four medical image understanding benchmarks that cover dermoscopy, chest radiographs, multi-image clinical cases, and biomedical figures [39, 50, 52, 55] demonstrate the superiority of MedJev-4B over the competing baselines. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B improves the average accuracy by an absolute 7.93%, from 61.13% to 69.06%, and accelerates end-to-end inference by 6.04, from 685.03 ms to 113.44 ms, with accuracy gains on every benchmark. These gains need no task-specific output head, because single model scores candidate sets that range from binary chest radiograph decision to seven-way dermoscopic diagnosis. The speedup tracks what generation would have cost, so it peaks on the multi-image benchmark, whose cases drive generative model to the longest responses of the four. In addition, comparison with 20 off-the-shelf general and medical VLMs (Fig. 1 (c)) shows that MedJev-4B is the only model at the 4B9B scale that is both the most accurate and the fastest on average. The main contribution of this paper is threefold: We introduce MedJev, system one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in single forward pass, without any autoregressive generation. We design language-side depth reduction that removes the computation decision does not need while keeping every visual token, and residual decision head that refines pretrained querykey matching with lightweight zero-initialized MLP for accurate decisions. On four medical image understanding benchmarks, MedJev-4B improves the average accuracy of Qwen3.5-4B by an absolute 7.93% with 6.04 end-to-end speedup, and achieves state-ofthe-art accuracy and speed among 4B9B general-purpose and medical VLMs. 2. Related Work 2.1. Medical Vision-Language Models Medical VLMs largely inherit the generative design of general-purpose VLMs and adapt it to clinical data. Early models tune LLaVA [24] on biomedical figure-caption pairs [20], learn from interleaved medical images and text [28], or train one generalist model across many medical tasks and modalities [40, 45]. Later models scale up instruction data and backbones [5, 34, 48], while strong general-purpose VLMs [3, 4, 19, 43] have also become competitive baselines on medical tasks. Inspired by chain-of-thought prompting [44] and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards [11], recent work further trains medical VLMs to write out reasoning steps before the answer [17, 29]. These models are evaluated on benchmarks that range from mix of closed and open questions [12, 18, 22] to multiple-choice questions over given candidates [14, 52, 55], yet all of them deliver their decisions as generated text. Because the decision arrives inside sentence, these benchmarks recover it by matching strings or by asking separate judge model, and response that states the right finding in an unexpected form can still be scored wrong. Contrastive models such as BiomedCLIP [54] instead score an image against text labels directly, but they encode the two modalities separately and cannot condition the scores on question or on several images. MedJev combines both families by keeping the joint multimodal processing of VLM while replacing text generation with direct decision. 2.2. Efficient Vision-Language Inference The inference cost of VLM comes mainly from long visual token sequences, the depth of the language model, and autoregressive decoding. Token reduction methods discard or merge visual tokens [6, 35, 47, 51, 56], which shortens the input but risks removing small medical findings. Layer 3 MedJev Figure 2 Overview of MedJev. Decoding also leaves the cost of single answer open, since model may spend few tokens or several hundred on the same question. generated answer carries the decision inside open-ended text, so the decision shares the parameters and the computation of captioning and dialogue. System one models [2] instead remove decoding and return typed decisions, and concurrent work extends them to images [53, 57], videos [59], spatial reasoning [30], histopathology [38], and ophthalmic cases [23]. Among them, MJev-Spatial [30] reads candidate scores from the native query and key projections at the top of the full language stack, while earlier work scores option letters with the language model head [33]. MedJev removes decoding and the upper language layers together, keeps every visual token, and and refines the pretrained querykey matching with zero-initialized residual head. 3. Baselines We compare MedJev-4B with 20 off-the-shelf vision-language models at the 4B to 9B scale. Fifteen of them are general-purpose models from the LLaVA [19, 25, 26], InternVL [7, 43, 58], Keye-VL [16, 49], MiMo-VL [46], and Qwen [3, 4, 32] families, and four are medical models trained on biomedical image-text data [5, 20, 34, 48]. The remaining one is the original Qwen3.5-4B [31], which we compare against most closely because it shares the vision encoder, the connector, and the retained language layers with MedJev-4B. Every baseline runs off the shelf with its official weights and chat template, and response naming no candidate counts as an error. We restrict the comparison to the 4B to 9B range so that every baseline stays close to MedJev-4B in size. 4.1.3. In Qwen3.5, the query projection also produces an output gate, which we discard. Conclusion In this paper, we presented MedJev, system one vision-language decision model for fast and effective medical image understanding. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B further employs languageside depth reduction and residual decision head for low latency and accurate candidate scoring. Across extensive experiments on four medical benchmarks, the effectiveness and the efficiency of MedJev-4B are fully validated. In the future, we plan to extend our work to more general scenarios such as general vision-language decision models and complex visual perception tasks.

Introduction to the Datasets We evaluate on four medical image understanding benchmarks. They differ in imaging modality, in the number of images case carries, and in whether the candidates are fixed label set or free text, and the number of candidates per example ranges from two to seven. HAM10000 [39]. Dermoscopic images of pigmented skin lesions, each labelled with one of seven diagnostic categories. The categories are melanoma, melanocytic nevus, basal cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis or intraepithelial carcinoma, benign keratosis, dermatofibroma and vascular lesion. We use the dermoscopic images as the training pool and the ISIC 2018 Task 3 split as the labelled test set, which holds 1,512 cases. The categories are imbalanced, with melanocytic nevus covering most cases. PneumoniaMNIST [50]. Pediatric chest radiographs at 224 224 from MedMNIST, to be classified as normal or pneumonia. We use the official split, which holds 4,708 training and 624 test images. MedThinkVQA [52]. Clinical cases drawn from radiological case reports, each presenting 2 to 47 images with question and five candidate diagnoses. The split holds 7,347 training and 720 test cases, and the test cases carry 5,845 images in total, 8.12 per case on average. PMC-VQA [55]. Questions about figures from the biomedical literature, each with four candidate answers written as free text and not drawn from label set. We use version 2 of the dataset, whose test split holds 33,430 question-answer pairs over 29,021 figures. Preprocessing. An example is kept when every image of it decodes, when it offers between two and seven candidates, and when the reference answer matches exactly one candidate. After these filters the four benchmarks contribute 174,360 training and 36,286 test examples, as listed in Tab. A1. B. Introduction to the Baselines We compare against 20 off-the-shelf vision-language models at the 4B to 9B scale, and separately against six released decision models. Every baseline runs with its official weights and its own chat template, and each is timed in its own session under the protocol of Sec. C. General Vision-Language Models. Fifteen models come from five families. From LLaVA we take LLaVA-1.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-Vicuna-7B, LLaVA-1.6-Mistral-7B and LLaVA-OneVision-7B [19, 25, 26]. From InternVL we take InternVL2.5-4B, InternVL3-9B, InternVL3.5-4B and InternVL3.5-8B [7, 43, 58]. From Keye-VL we take Keye-VL-8B-Preview and Keye-VL-1.5-8B [16, 49], and from MiMo-VL we take MiMo-VL-7B-RL [46]. From Qwen we take Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B [3, 4, 32], four models that span two generations. Medical Vision-Language Models. Four models are trained on biomedical image-text data. They are LLaVA-Med-v1.5-7B [20], HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B [5], MedGemma-4B [34] and Lingshu-7B [48]. The Backbone. Qwen3.5-4B [31] is the model MedJev-4B is built from. It shares the vision encoder, the connector and the retained language layers, and it is timed in the same session as MedJev-4B. Released Decision Models. Six systems share the decision interface. Two of them are medical, OmniMed-Jev-4B [37] and PathJev-P [38], both on MedGemma-1.5-4B backbone. Prompt and Markers. request is laid out as the visual tokens of every image, the question, question marker, then each candidate followed by an option marker, and finally decision marker. The backbone of Qwen3.5-4B [31] has 32 language layers. We keep layers 1 to 23 complete, delete layers 24 to 31 entirely, and keep from layer 32 only the query and key projections that the matching term needs. The last layer of Qwen3.5 is full-attention layer and supplies the matching space. Its query projection also emits an output gate, which we discard. Training. single model is trained for one epoch over the 174,360 training examples of the four benchmarks, which is 5,449 updates at global batch size of 32. The loss is cross-entropy over the candidates of each example, weighted so that no benchmark dominates and, within each classification benchmark, so that no diagnosis dominates. Each benchmark first receives the same total weight, which scales an example by the pooled training size over four times its own, from 4.38 on HAM10000 to 0.29 on PMC-VQA. Within benchmark, classification example is weighted by the inverse of its observed class frequency and question-answering examples count equally.
